threads.thread_goal: Align on pilot scope, client selection, and overall approach.

messages.text: Kicking off the Integrated Home Care Safety and Hygiene Improvement Pilot for project_pack_ref: Integrated Home Care Safety and Hygiene Improvement Pilot. Goal is to have a standard routine ready to pilot within 21 days, without extending visit times or adding staff. We need to align on: 1) which clients go into the pilot and their visit schedule for A8, and 2) what must be in scope for the home visit safety and hygiene checklist for T1 and A1. I suggest we start with around 5–8 clients with mixed needs (mobility support, dietary restrictions, allergy history) so T2 can capture a good range of instruction sheets. @home care aide and @shelf filler roles, can you help propose clients and flag any constraints from your side before we lock D1 and D2

Thanks for starting this. From recent visits, I can think of five clients who would give us a good spread for A8: 1) Two with mobility limitations and regular morning hygiene support. 2) One with strict dietary needs and food allergies. 3) One with cognitive decline where routines are very fixed. 4) One family that already asks a lot of questions about cleaning products. For T2, I can start drafting instruction sheets for these five based on current notes and what we already know about diet, allergies, and routines. Before we confirm D1, do we want to cap at five clients for the first two weeks, or aim for more if scheduling allows

Five sounds manageable to start, especially if we want aides to actually use the checklist from T1 in every visit without feeling overloaded. We can always add more clients later if the first week goes smoothly. For A8, we should log for each pilot client: name or code, address, usual visit days and times, and main risk points (for example falls, choking risk, allergy triggers). That will help us later when we look at incidents and near-misses. I can help structure A8 once we agree on the list of clients for D1.

From the storage and supplies side, starting with five clients is easier. It keeps the hygiene kit demand small while we test the restocking rules later in T4. For A8, it would help me if we also note which clients have very limited storage space at home. That way we do not send a full kit where there is nowhere to keep it. I can add a simple storage-notes column once the client list is confirmed.

On the checklist scope for T1 and A1, I was thinking we cover: before entering the home, hand hygiene and basic PPE check; during the visit, surface cleaning around care activities and safe handling of linens; and before leaving, waste disposal and quick check that products are stored safely. I am not sure how much detail we can fit on one page though. Maybe we should leave out some of the more advanced disinfection steps for now and just focus on the basics that fit into the current visit time.

Good starting point. To keep A1 to one page as required in T1, I suggest we group by visit phase and keep each step short. For scope, I think we must include at least: 1) Hand hygiene moments and glove use. 2) Cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces around the client. 3) Linen handling and laundry bag rules. 4) Basic first aid readiness check, like where the kit is and if anything is missing. Anything beyond that, like deep cleaning, might be out of scope for this pilot. @home care aide, does that feel realistic within current visit slots, or are we missing something critical

From the visit side, that list is workable if we keep each step very concrete. I would add one more area to the scope for A1: safe food handling when we prepare or reheat meals, especially for clients with dietary restrictions that will be documented in A2 and T2. That can be just a few checks, like separate utensils for raw and cooked food and checking expiry dates. If we keep it to those five blocks, I think it still fits on one page and into the visit time.

Agree on adding a short food handling section. It also links well with the dietary and allergy information in A2 from T2. To avoid overload, we can phrase each block as 3–5 bullet points max. For example, for linen handling we can cover: separate clean and dirty, use a bag for transport, and wash at appropriate temperature if done on site. That should keep A1 practical.

On the food handling part, just a note from the supplies angle: if we expect aides to separate utensils or use specific cleaning products for kitchen surfaces, we should make sure those items are part of the hygiene kit later in T4 and reflected in the storage checklist A7. Otherwise the checklist A1 will ask for steps that are not possible in some homes.

I can start a draft of A1 under T1 using the five blocks we listed: hand hygiene and gloves, high-touch surfaces, linen handling, basic first aid readiness, and safe food handling. I will keep it to one page and group by before, during, and after the visit. Once we confirm the pilot client list for A8, I can also check if any of them have special product sensitivities so we do not include steps that conflict with their allergies.

On the client list for D1, I propose we confirm the five you suggested for A8: 1) Two mobility support clients with regular morning visits. 2) One with strict diet and known food allergies. 3) One with cognitive decline and fixed routines. 4) One family very engaged on cleaning and product questions. We will log their visit days and times plus main risk points in A8. If no one objects by tomorrow, we will treat this as the confirmed pilot set for the first two weeks.

No objections from me. I will start T2 for these five clients and structure A2 so that diet, allergies, mobility, and daily routines are clearly separated. That will also help when we map the checklist A1 steps to each client, for example where food handling is relevant versus where it is not.

To close D2 on the checklist scope, let me restate what we are including in A1 under T1: 1) Hand hygiene and glove use at key moments. 2) Cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces around the client. 3) Linen handling and laundry bag rules. 4) Basic first aid readiness check. 5) Safe food handling where applicable, linked to A2. We are explicitly not including deep cleaning or tasks that would extend visit time beyond current slots. If everyone agrees, we can treat this as the final scope for the first draft.
This scope works for me and fits with what we can realistically support with supplies later. Keeping deep cleaning out of scope for now is a good call, especially with the budget cap.

Agreed on the scope. I will make sure the draft of A1 under T1 sticks to these five areas and stays within one page. Once I have a first version, I will share it in the channel for comments before we move to training materials.

Great, then we will proceed with those five clients for A8 and the agreed checklist scope for A1. I will draft a simple structure for A8 with client codes, visit schedule, main risks, and storage notes so @shelf filler can add supply-related details later. That will set us up for the pilot planning in T6.

threads.thread_goal: Design and finalize the safety checklist and training materials.

messages.text: I have a first draft of the Home Visit Safety and Hygiene Checklist for T1, which will become A1. It is one page, grouped by before, during, and after the visit, and covers the five areas we agreed in D2: hand hygiene and gloves, high-touch surfaces, linen handling, basic first aid readiness, and safe food handling linked to A2. Before we call this version 1.0, I would like feedback on whether any steps are unclear or unrealistic in real visits. Once A1 is stable, we can align T5 and A3 so the training mini-guide matches the checklist.

I walked through the draft A1 against two of the pilot clients from A8. Overall it fits into the visit flow. A few detailed comments: 1) Before visit: the hand hygiene step is clear, but we might want to add a quick reminder about removing rings or bracelets that can tear gloves. 2) During visit: the high-touch surfaces list is good, but maybe we should specify a maximum of three priority surfaces per visit so aides do not feel they must clean everything. 3) Food handling: for clients without meal prep, we should have a simple 'not applicable' option so aides do not feel they are skipping something. None of this changes the scope from D2, just makes it easier to follow.

From a product safety angle, the wording in A1 should stay neutral about specific brands, since T3 will define the approved product list. For example, instead of naming a disinfectant, we can say 'use approved surface disinfectant from the hygiene kit' and then A3 can explain what that means. Also, for linen handling, we might want to add a short note about checking for visible contamination and handling those items separately, which is still feasible within the visit time.

These are good refinements. To keep A1 concise, I suggest we: 1) Add a short note under hand hygiene about removing jewelry that interferes with glove use. 2) For high-touch surfaces, add a line like 'focus on up to three priority surfaces agreed with the client or family'. 3) For food handling, include a checkbox 'not applicable for this visit'. None of this adds new sections, so we stay within the scope from D2 and the one-page limit in T1.

On the neutral wording, that will also help when we build the hygiene kit and storage plan in A4 and A7. If A1 just says 'approved surface disinfectant', we can manage substitutions in T4 and T3 without having to reprint the checklist every time a product changes.

I will update A1 under T1 with those three changes and the neutral wording for products. I will also double-check that the language matches what aides see in A2 for dietary and allergy notes, so there is no confusion when they switch between documents during a visit.

Once you update A1, I can do a quick run-through in a mock visit and time how long it takes to follow all steps for one of the more complex clients from A8. If it still fits within the usual slot, I would be comfortable calling this version 1.0 for the pilot.

In parallel, I can start outlining A3 for T5 so the training mini-guide mirrors the structure of A1: before, during, and after the visit, with short examples of correct and incorrect practices. For example, a small scenario on how to handle a spill on the floor without creating a slip risk, or how to manage a client who refuses a certain cleaning product due to smell.

For A3, I recommend we keep it to a short mini-guide, maybe 3–4 pages, focusing on: 1) Why we are changing the routine and how it helps clients and aides. 2) Key safety points from A1, including allergy checks linked to A2. 3) Simple examples of good and poor practice. 4) A short section on how to log incidents using A5, so we connect T5 and T7. We also need to decide on the training format for D4: short group session, one-to-one, or self-study with follow-up questions.

From the aides perspective, a short group session works best, ideally 45–60 minutes, with time to ask questions and practice using A1 and A2 on real cases. We can then leave A3 as a reference document. For those who cannot attend, we could record the session and share it, but I would not rely only on self-study if we want consistent adoption.

If we go with a group session, it would be helpful to include a short part on how aides should request supplies or flag stock issues, so they know how A4 and A7 work in practice. That way, when something is missing, they know the process instead of improvising with whatever is at hand.

I have applied the edits to A1 and checked that it still fits on one page. The steps are grouped clearly and there is a 'not applicable' option for food handling. Unless the timing test shows a problem, I think this is ready to be treated as version 1.0 for the pilot under T1.

I just did a dry run with A1 for one of the more complex clients. Following all relevant steps added about three minutes to the visit, which is acceptable. With practice, it should be even faster. From my side, I am comfortable calling this A1 version 1.0 for the pilot.

I have now drafted A3 under T5 with the structure we discussed and included a short section on incident logging with A5. It explains why the changes are needed, highlights key safety points from A1, and gives simple examples of correct and incorrect practices. For the format, I support the 45–60 minute group session, with A3 shared afterwards and a recording for those who cannot attend.

To close D4, I propose we approve A3 as the training mini-guide for the pilot and confirm the training format as: one 60-minute group session for all aides involved in the pilot, using A1, A2, and A3, plus a recording and the guide shared in the channel for anyone who cannot attend. If there are no objections by tomorrow, we will treat this as agreed.
No objections from me. With A1 approved as version 1.0 and A3 ready, we can schedule the group session next week so aides are trained before we start T6.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in supply list, hygiene kit contents, and storage setup.

messages.text: I have put together a proposal for the minimal home care hygiene kit for T4, which will feed into A4. It is based on the checklist A1 and the pilot client list in A8. The kit includes: 1) Hand hygiene: alcohol-based hand rub and a small pack of disposable towels. 2) Surface cleaning: multi-surface cleaner and an approved disinfectant from the list that will come from T3. 3) Linen handling: disposable gloves and laundry bags. 4) Food handling: kitchen-safe cleaner where meal prep is part of the visit. I also drafted restocking rules and some initial storage and labeling ideas that link to A7 and T8. I would like feedback before we finalize D5 and D6.

From the product safety side under T3, we need to make sure the disinfectant and cleaners in A4 are compatible with common household surfaces and have clear allergy notes. I will review candidate products and propose 3–5 core items with usage instructions. For the pilot, we should avoid anything with strong fragrances, given the risk of sensitivities mentioned in the project risks.

The structure of the kit in A4 looks aligned with A1. One concern is storage space in some homes from A8. For clients with very limited space, could we define a 'core kit' and an 'optional add-on' so we do not overload them with products they rarely use

Yes, that matches what I had in mind. For A4 under T4, I can define: 1) A core kit that every pilot client gets, covering hand hygiene, basic surface cleaning, gloves, and laundry bags. 2) An optional add-on for food handling and any extra items needed for specific clients, based on A2 and A8. I will also list acceptable substitutes for each item so we can handle stock issues without breaking the routine.

From the visit side, the proposed kit seems manageable to carry, as long as we keep packaging compact. For storage in the home, some families already have a small cleaning corner; others do not. It would help if A7 under T8 includes a simple suggestion like 'store kit in a cool, dry place away from children and pets', plus a label that makes it easy to spot quickly during a visit.

I will finalize the safe product list for T3 with 3–5 core products and share it so you can plug the exact product codes and substitutes into A4. I will also add notes on which surfaces to avoid and any allergy warnings, so we can reflect that in both A1 and A3 where needed.

For A7 and T8, I propose we map the storage areas used by aides at the base location and, where possible, agree with families on a dedicated spot in the home. Labels will show the product name, code, and a simple icon (for example hand, surface, linen, kitchen) so aides can find items quickly. For out-of-stock alerts, we can use a simple note in the incident log A5 or a short weekly message in this channel.

Using A5 for stock alerts is creative, but we should be careful not to mix safety incidents with supply issues. Maybe we keep A5 for incidents and near-misses only, and use a simple shared note or weekly check-in for stock. We can still mention in A3 how aides should report missing items.

Good point. I will keep A5 strictly for safety incidents and near-misses. For stock-outs, I will add a simple process in A4 and A7: aides note missing items on a small restocking sheet at the base, and we review it in a weekly planning message. That keeps things separate and easier to track.

I have completed the review for T3. The approved list includes: 1) One alcohol-based hand rub. 2) One neutral multi-surface cleaner. 3) One low-fragrance disinfectant compatible with most household surfaces. 4) One kitchen-safe cleaner. For each, I documented usage instructions, allergy considerations, and surface compatibility. This can now be integrated into A4 and referenced in A1 and A3.

Great, I will now finalize A4 under T4 with the core kit and optional add-ons, including product codes and acceptable substitutes based on your T3 list. I will also estimate kit cost to ensure we stay within the pilot budget and add the restocking rules we discussed.

Once A4 is ready, I can quickly check it against the instruction sheets in A2 for the five pilot clients to see if any special needs are missing, for example fragrance-free options or extra gloves for wound care visits.

I have also drafted A7 under T8. It maps the shelves at the base, defines where each kit item sits, and includes label text and icons. For homes, it suggests a small box or basket where possible, with a simple label like 'home care hygiene kit'. I think this is enough to support the pilot without major changes to existing storage.

To close D5, I propose we approve the hygiene kit contents and restocking rules in A4 as the final version for the pilot: core kit plus optional add-ons, with product codes, substitutes, and weekly restocking based on the base restocking sheet. If there are no objections by tomorrow, we will treat A4 as approved for the pilot.
No objections from me. The kit contents in A4 cover what we need to follow A1 in the five pilot homes, and the restocking rules are simple enough to follow.

For D6, I suggest we agree that: 1) At the base, pilot supplies are stored on the mapped shelves with labels from A7. 2) In homes, we use a small box or basket where possible, labeled as 'home care hygiene kit' as described in A7. 3) Aides will be shown these locations during training and asked to keep them consistent. If everyone is aligned, we can treat this as the approved storage and labeling approach for the pilot.
Aligned from my side. This setup is realistic to implement and should make it easy for aides to find what they need quickly.

threads.thread_goal: Coordinate pilot execution, incident logging, and quick fixes.

messages.text: Today we start the pilot visits using the new checklist A1 and the client instruction sheets A2 for the five clients listed in A8 under T6. Aides should now use A1 in every visit for these clients and follow the hygiene kit setup from A4 and A7. We also need to align on how and when to log incidents and near-misses using A5 under T7, so we can close D7. Please share any early issues from the first visits and thoughts on a practical logging routine.

Quick update from the morning visits under T6: 1) A1 worked smoothly for three clients; the 'not applicable' option for food handling helped. 2) For one client, the family had moved some of the kit items, so it took extra time to find them. 3) No incidents so far, but I had one near-miss where a client almost tripped over a bucket left in the hallway. I noted it in my own notes for now. For A5, I would prefer a simple digital form we can fill at the end of the day rather than during the visit, otherwise it will be hard to stay on schedule.

I had one visit this afternoon. A1 was fine, but I was not sure whether to log a minor skin redness after using the disinfectant as an incident in A5 or just as a note in the client sheet A2. The client said it was only a little itchy and it went away after rinsing. We might need clearer guidance in A3 and A5 on what counts as an incident versus a minor observation.

For product-related reactions, even mild ones, I would prefer we log them in A5 during the pilot so we can see patterns. In A3 we can clarify that any unexpected skin, breathing, or eye reaction after product use should be logged as an incident, even if it resolves quickly. We can also add a field in A5 to note severity, so we can distinguish minor from serious cases.

On the kit being moved, that is exactly where the labeling from A7 should help. Maybe we need to remind families during visits that the 'home care hygiene kit' box should stay in the agreed place. If this keeps happening, we might add a short note in A2 for those clients about preferred storage location.

On D7, I propose the following routine for A5 under T7: 1) Aides note any incidents or near-misses on paper or in their own notes during the visit if needed. 2) At the end of each day, they complete one A5 entry per event in a simple digital form, taking about 3–5 minutes. 3) We keep A5 focused on safety and hygiene events: falls or near-falls, product reactions, contamination risks, missing critical supplies, and similar. We can then review logs weekly. Does this feel realistic for you

Yes, that routine is workable. End-of-day logging in A5 is much more realistic than trying to fill forms in the middle of visits. It would help if the form is short, with checkboxes for common event types and a small free-text field. I can test the template once T7 is ready.

I will adjust A5 under T7 so it has: 1) Event type with checkboxes (fall, near-fall, product reaction, contamination risk, missing critical supply, other). 2) Short description and cause. 3) Follow-up actions taken. 4) Severity level. I will also create one test entry to confirm the process works, as required in T7.

Understood. I will log the skin redness case in A5 as a minor product reaction and note that it resolved after rinsing. It would be helpful if A3 includes one example like this so aides know what to do step by step.

Once A5 is updated, we should also remind aides during the daily async check-in to mention if they logged any events that day. That will help us spot patterns early without waiting for the end of the pilot.

Daily check-in from today: 1) Two visits completed with A1 and A2, no incidents. 2) One near-miss with a slippery bathroom floor; I will log it in A5 tonight. 3) One family asked if we could use a different fragrance for the disinfectant; I noted it in A2 and will see if it matches any allergy notes.

On the fragrance question, if it is just a preference and not an allergy, we might not be able to change products during the pilot due to T3 and stock constraints. But if A2 or A5 shows repeated discomfort, we can look at alternatives within the approved list.
Agreed. For now, log any strong reactions in A5 and note preferences in A2. At the end of the pilot, T9 will help us see if we need to adjust the product list in T3 for the wider rollout.

To formalize D7, we will use A5 as the standard incident and near-miss log for the pilot under T7, with aides completing entries at the end of each day for any relevant events during T6 visits. A5 will be limited to safety and hygiene events, and we will remind aides in the daily async check-in to mention if they logged anything. Unless there are objections, this will be our agreed logging process for the pilot.
Aligned on the logging process. I will start using A5 this evening for the near-miss and any other events, and mention it in the daily check-ins.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on adjustments and rollout plan.

messages.text: I have drafted the pilot evaluation summary for T12, which will become A6. It covers objectives, approach, results, and key metrics from T9, including incident data from A5, feedback from aides and families, and how well A1, A2, and A4 worked in practice. Overall, incidents were low but we saw recurring themes: 1) A few near-falls related to wet floors. 2) Several mild skin reactions to one disinfectant. 3) Some confusion about where kits were stored in homes. I would like your input on the proposed recommendations before we decide on D8 for wider rollout.

From the aide side, the summary in A6 matches my experience. A1 became easier to use after a few days, and families appreciated the clearer routines. The main pain points were: 1) Remembering to check kit storage in each home. 2) Explaining product changes to families who were used to their own cleaners. For T10, I would suggest we tweak A1 to highlight floor drying steps more clearly and add a short reminder about explaining product use to families.

I agree with the main findings. One thing I noticed is that some aides skipped parts of A1 when they felt rushed, especially the first aid readiness check. Maybe in T10 we can simplify that section or move some checks to a weekly routine instead of every visit.

On supplies, A4 and A7 mostly worked, but we had a few stock-outs of gloves and laundry bags. The restocking sheet helped, but we underestimated usage for clients with more intensive care. For T11, I recommend we adjust the stocking plan to slightly higher minimum levels for those items and note the cost impact in A6 so stakeholders see the trade-off.

On the product reactions, A5 shows that most were mild but clustered around one disinfectant. For the rollout, we might want to switch to an alternative from the approved list in T3 or at least restrict that product to homes where no reactions were reported. We should capture this clearly in A6 and adjust A4 and A3 accordingly.

I can update the product list under T3 to mark that disinfectant as second choice and promote a better-tolerated option as the default for the rollout. We will then update A4 and A3 to reflect this, and note the change in A6 as a key recommendation.

For T10, I can take the lead on adjusting A1 and A2 based on the top improvement points from T9 and A6: 1) Make floor drying and slip prevention more visible. 2) Simplify first aid readiness to a shorter checklist, maybe once per week. 3) Add a short script in A2 for explaining new products to families. I will then ask one of you to validate the changes before we finalize.

For T11, I will update the supply list and stocking plan to: 1) Increase baseline glove and laundry bag quantities for clients with higher care intensity. 2) Adjust restocking triggers so we act before we hit zero. 3) Add a short note on cost changes in A6 so stakeholders see that the increase is modest compared to the safety benefits.

When you update A1 and A2 under T10, I can review them from the perspective of someone who used them in the pilot and check that the changes are easy to explain to newer aides. We should also highlight the changes clearly so training for the rollout can focus on what is new.

I will validate the revised A1 and A2 once you complete T10, checking that the top five improvement points from T9 and A6 are addressed and that the documents stay aligned with the updated product list and supply plan.

Looking at A6 and the data from T9, my view is that the pilot met its main objectives: incidents were low, routines became more consistent, and most feedback from families was positive once they understood the changes. We have clear adjustments identified for A1, A2, A3, and A4. I am inclined to recommend a go for wider rollout, with the condition that we implement the listed adjustments first.
I support a go for wider rollout, as long as we adjust the checklist and supplies as discussed and plan a short refresher training using A3 for all aides, not just those in the pilot.
From the supply and storage side, I also support rollout. The adjustments in T11 are manageable and the cost increase is reasonable compared to the reduction in risk we saw in A6.

Given the alignment here, I will finalize A6 under T12 with a clear recommendation to proceed with wider rollout, listing the required adjustments and next steps. This will include references to the updated A1, A2, A3, and A4, and the revised stocking plan from T11.

To close D8, we agree to approve the final recommendations in A6 and proceed with a wider rollout, conditional on completing T10 and T11 updates and a short refresher training using A3. A6 will serve as the reference for stakeholders, and we will share it in this channel for formal sign-off.
Sounds good. I will start on T10 so we can have the updated A1 and A2 ready before the refresher training.
